newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac pays glowing tribute to Harriman.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac pays glowing tribute to Harriman.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac paid glowing tribute on Saturday to the late U.S. ambassador Pamela Harriman at a leave-taking ceremony which drew a discreet veil over Franco-American tensions.

The French head of state, senior U.S. officials including National Security Advisor Samuel Berger, and relatives gathered to recall the glittering past and the four-year Paris tenure of Harriman, who died on Wednesday of a brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

Highlighting their common revolutionary legacy, both U.S. Marines and French Republican Guards stood watch in crisp sunshine over Harriman's wooden coffin, draped in the Stars and Stripes and placed on the garden terrace of the embassy residence.

Drawing his wife Bernadette to his side, a grim-faced Chirac paused silently before the casket before addressing guests including Italian magnate Gianni Agnelli, one of the many wealthy and powerful men Harriman was linked to as wife or companion.

"Two centuries ago, Benjamin Franklin and then Thomas Jefferson represented in Paris a nascent America. In 1993, President Bill Clinton chose an exceptional person to follow in their footsteps," Chirac said in a speech.

"To say that she was an exceptional representative of the United States in France does not do justice to her achievement: she lent to our longstanding alliance the radiant strength of her personality. She was elegance itself. She was grace."
Harriman was "also a peerless diplomat", indispensible to both Clinton and himself in helping find the way forward to agreement, Chirac said.

During her time as ambassador, Paris and Washington sparred over alleged U.S. espionage, the "Europeanisation" of NATO, leadership of the United Nations, influence in Middle East peacemaking and power rivalry in Africa.

Chirac placed on the coffin the red sash of the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour. He told her a month ago that he planned to give her France's highest award. "It is my great regret that the ceremony has become a last leave-taking."

Guests invited to the ceremony, organised by Harriman's family, included U.S. Congressman Thomas Foley, French singer Line Renaud, the wife of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, and Maurice Druon, secretary of the French Academy.

Harriman's son Winston Spencer Churchill, a British member of parliament, thanked Chirac for attending and said his mother "put her heart and energy into...forging better France-US relations, even if this was not always easy".
Berger praised Harriman as "an invaluable bridge of communication and understanding between our leaders and our people. Like any friendship, our relationship requires nurturing and attention."
As the cortege snaked its way through the gardens to the rolling of drums, embassy chefs and waiters in white aprons and jackets stood on the lawn to watch.
Afterwards, guests who filed out through the residence admired some of the finest pieces in Harriman's private art collection, including works by Renoir, Cezanne and De Chirico.
The family, and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette representing France, followed the body to Orly airport from where a USAF Boeing 707 flight took off at 1330 local (1230 GMT) bound for Washington.
Harriman will be buried at Arden House in New York State, former residence of her husband, the late New York governor and U.S. diplomat Averell Harriman.
